output.myth: Ennu the Kite-Wright made the first bridled kite for Aun, who asked how a thing might hold still in a gale. She cut the cloth from an old sail, stretched it on whalebone, and tied one knot in the bridle so the wind would have something to pull against. Tavo the Gale came down the cliff laughing and tore off the tail in one shake. So Ennu tied long ribbons to the corners and let them hang. A kite that is all sail goes nowhere, she said; it needs weight to hang from. Aun flew it until the line ran out, which is how he learned the sky was far. When he cut the string, that kite went aloft first, and it still hangs over Vel with its ribbons trailing toward the islands. Hesk counts the knots on the Reel and says the bridle is still tied. Hang your ribbons low when you fly. The wind reads them.
output.verse:
Hang your ribbons low
the wind reads them where they fall
Ennu's knot still holds
